title: Heat gave no clear added prediction gain at known Atlantic and Pacific reef sites in 2011-2019
abstract: We tested whether measured heat stress improved later-year predictions of any reported coral bleaching beyond site history, calendar month and depth. Models trained in 2003-2010 were fixed for four Atlantic and Pacific tests in 2011-2014 and 2015-2019. The tests used 992 surveys at 204 known sites. Adding heat increased Brier loss slightly in both early tests and reduced it in both late tests. All four adjusted uncertainty intervals included zero. Alternative penalty strengths and a one-percent outcome gave no clear common gain. The known-site rule excluded 3,838 otherwise eligible later surveys. Only 35 test surveys had heat dose at least four degree-heating weeks. Thus the result is a narrow prediction benchmark, not evidence that heat is unimportant. Few years and regions, selected visits, missing reports and retrospective climate norms limit inference. The package gives source hashes, event evidence, fitted models, predictions, code, uncertainty checks and a figure.

display.caption: Heat-model minus baseline Brier loss and calibration in the mean. Bars use approximate four-test adjusted intervals with year and ecological-region score variances. Negative loss differences favor heat. Models were fit only in 2003-2010. Selected known-site tests have limited high-heat support.
